subsystems.name: Structural shell
subsystems.role: carries the building's own weight plus the crushing force of the vacuum layer around it.

subsystems.name: Vacuum envelope
subsystems.role: removes the air between shells so heat cannot move by conduction or convection.
parts: micro-support pillars or hollow glass microspheres

subsystems.name: Thermal control
subsystems.role: a vacuum blocks conduction but not radiation, so waste heat from people, lighting and machines still has to be dumped.

subsystems.name: Life support and atmosphere
subsystems.role: keeps the interior breathable and near-closed-loop for months at a time.

subsystems.name: Power
subsystems.role: runs pumps, life support, lighting and growing lights.
parts: solar arrays or small nuclear reactors

subsystems.name: Habitation and food
subsystems.role: living volume plus food production inside the shell.

subsystems.name: Airlocks and logistics
subsystems.role: lets people and goods pass without breaking the vacuum.

buildSteps.title: Study site and shape
buildSteps.detail: Choose a location with stable ground and useful sun, then fix the shell geometry so the vacuum gap can resist atmospheric pressure everywhere.

buildSteps.title: Make the shells
buildSteps.detail: Composite panels and curved segments are laid up with carbon-nanotube-reinforced resin, cured in large moulds, and individually leak-tested.

buildSteps.title: Erect the inner pressure shell
buildSteps.detail: Segments are assembled and sealed into a continuous airtight envelope, then proof-tested at full internal pressure.

buildSteps.title: Fit the vacuum core
buildSteps.detail: Micro-support pillars or glass microspheres are placed across the gap so the two shells cannot collapse into each other, and low-emissivity coatings are applied.

buildSteps.title: Close the outer shell
buildSteps.detail: The outer skin is fixed over the supports, forming a sealed sandwich, with all pipes, cables and doors routed through sealed sleeves.

buildSteps.title: Pump down and outgas
buildSteps.detail: Air is pumped out of the gap; the structure is warmed and vented repeatedly to drive off trapped moisture and volatiles, then getters absorb what remains.

buildSteps.title: Commission the services
buildSteps.detail: Life support, thermal loops, power and airlocks are started and balanced while the shell is monitored for leaks.

buildSteps.title: Verify over a full year
buildSteps.detail: Leak rate, heat loss and air quality are logged through a complete seasonal cycle before anyone lives there permanently.

prerequisites.why: individual nanotubes are very strong, but bulk fibres lose most of that strength and no load-bearing shell of this kind has been made.
vacuum-insulated panels and vacuum glazing exist, but only in fixed, factory-made panel sizes.
today's vacuum systems are continuously pumped and serviced; a city-sized shell would have to stay sealed for decades.
the technology has been demonstrated in orbit for small crews, not for thousands of people with fully closed food and water cycles.
Antarctic stations and offshore platforms show the pattern, but at a fraction of the scale and complexity.

pathway.milestone: vacuum-insulated panels and vacuum glazing used in ordinary buildings
pathway.unlocks: cheap, proven insulating components and sealing know-how.

pathway.milestone: vacuum-insulated modular habitats for polar stations and space use
pathway.unlocks: real-world data on micro-supports, leak rates and long-term seals at room scale.

pathway.milestone: one demonstration hall wrapped in a full vacuum envelope, instrumented for years
pathway.unlocks: evidence that a large shell can stay sealed and save enough energy to justify itself.

pathway.milestone: a multi-module arcology with shared vacuum envelope
pathway.unlocks: self-contained habitation in extreme environments — only if composite strength and seal life both improve by orders of magnitude.
